tip: 'Logo que' + present tense means 'as soon as.' It's very common in daily Brazilian Portuguese.
'A gente' means 'we' but takes the he/she verb form: 'a gente aluga', not 'alugamos'.
Weather and temperature use 'estar' because they change – 'o tempo está bom' (the weather is good right now).
After a motion verb, a bare infinitive shows purpose, with no 'para' needed: 'foi ao mercado comprar' = went to buy.
'À academia' uses the contraction 'à' (a + a) because 'academia' is feminine and 'ir a' requires the preposition 'a.'
'Passar em' means to stop by or drop by a place. It's one of the most common uses of 'passar' in everyday Brazilian Portuguese.
Masculine plural covers mixed groups: 'irmãos' means brothers, or siblings of both genders. An all-female set would be 'irmãs.'
'Quem' (who) as a subject normally takes a singular verb: 'quem cozinhou', even if more than one person might have cooked.
'Estar' plus an '-ndo' verb makes the present continuous: 'estou aprendendo' is 'I'm learning', an action underway right now.
'Simpática' means nice or friendly, not 'sympathetic.' It describes a warm, likeable person.
'A gente' means 'we' but takes a singular verb: 'a gente é,' never 'a gente somos.' It is the everyday spoken 'we.'
Portuguese uses 'estar com' + noun where English often uses 'to be' + adjective: 'estou com dor' (I'm in pain), 'estou com fome' (I'm hungry).
'Saudade' is a famously Portuguese word for a deep longing or missing. 'Estar com saudade de' is how you express missing someone or something.
Inherent traits take 'ser': 'a água do mar é salgada'. Salt is part of what seawater is, not a passing state.
'Ser' for origin: 'vocês são de onde?' Word order is flexible in questions – 'de onde vocês são?' also works.
Normally no article before a profession: 'ele é engenheiro,' not 'um engenheiro.' Portuguese drops the 'a/an' that English uses here.
For where a place is, Brazilians use 'ficar': 'onde fica o banheiro' means 'where is the bathroom', with 'ficar' marking a settled location.
'Dar aulas', literally 'to give classes', means to teach: 'dou aulas de português' is 'I teach Portuguese'.
'Ser' + 'de' for origin: 'nós somos de Belo Horizonte.' This is permanent identity, so use 'ser.'
'Ter medo de' means 'to be afraid of' – literally 'to have fear of.' Many English 'be' expressions use 'ter' in Portuguese.
Portuguese has an allergy rather than being allergic: 'tenho alergia a camarão' = I'm allergic to shrimp.
'Estar' plus an '-ndo' verb is English '-ing' in progress: 'estamos planejando' means 'we are planning'. Brazilians lean on it constantly.
Traffic conditions change daily – use 'estar.' If you said 'o trânsito é horrível,' you'd mean it's always terrible.
Comparatives normally just add 'mais' before the adjective: 'mais barato' = cheaper. No word ending changes.
'Ir a pé,' literally 'go by foot,' means to walk somewhere: 'a gente pode ir a pé.'
Portuguese asks 'qual é', not 'o que', for numbers and names: 'qual é o seu número'. It is 'which is' where English says 'what'.
'Fazer aniversário,' literally 'to make a birthday,' is how you say to have a birthday: 'faço aniversário em março.'
Days of the week take 'no/na' for 'on': 'no sábado' = on Saturday. There is no separate word for 'on.'
Emotion adjectives often take 'com' for the thing that caused them: 'surpreso com a notícia' (surprised by the news), where English uses by or at.
The room can be cleaned – the mess is a temporary state, so use 'estar.' If you said 'é uma bagunça,' you'd mean it's inherently messy.
